content.question: What limitation of LinearLayout did the instructor highlight at the start of Episode 2?

options.text: That to place elements left and right repeatedly you may end up writing many nested LinearLayouts and excessive code.
That LinearLayout cannot display images.
That LinearLayout always requires ConstraintSet to run.
That LinearLayout only supports vertical orientation on tablets.

content.explanation: He noted that using LinearLayout for every left/right arrangement often forces many nested layouts and more code; this motivated introducing RelativeLayout as an alternative.
hints: He asked whether you've found any limitation with LinearLayout.
He said placing right and left repeatedly forces lots of code.

content.question: What is the core idea behind RelativeLayout as explained in Episode 2?

options.text: It allows positioning components relative to each other or to the parent container (e.g., left of, right of, below).
It automatically lays out views in a grid without any attributes.
It requires orientation attribute like LinearLayout to operate.
It is only for drawing shapes and cannot contain child views.

content.explanation: RelativeLayout positions elements relative to each other or the parent (for example placing A to the left of B), avoiding repeated nested orientation-based layouts.
hints: He compared it to students A and B standing relative to each other.
Relative positions (left of, right of, below) are the main concept.

content.question: Which of these statements about RelativeLayout did the instructor imply is true?

options.text: RelativeLayout does not require an orientation attribute and instead relies on positional relationships.
RelativeLayout requires orientation='horizontal' to position elements left/right.
RelativeLayout automatically stacks children vertically like LinearLayout.
RelativeLayout is deprecated and should not be used.

content.explanation: He showed that unlike LinearLayout, RelativeLayout doesn't use orientation; positions are defined by relational attributes between views or relative to the parent.
hints: He removed orientation-related errors when replacing ConstraintLayout with RelativeLayout.
Relative layout centers on relations, not orientation.

content.question: In the instructor's analogy, if student A stands 'left of' student B, what concept does this represent in RelativeLayout?

options.text: Defining a view's position in relation to another view (e.g., android:layout_toLeftOf).
A new type of animation between students.
A memory leak scenario in layouts.
Specifying padding for both views simultaneously.

content.explanation: The analogy maps directly to RelativeLayout attributes like layout_toLeftOf or layout_toRightOf that position a view relative to another view.
hints: He used two students A and B to explain relative placement.
Think of attributes that say 'toLeftOf' or 'below'.

content.question: What caution did the instructor give about the grid lines used to explain positions?

options.text: The grid lines are imaginary conceptual aids and not features of Android Studio; don't try to add them in code.
The grid lines must be added as child views to the layout to work at runtime.
These grid lines are required to enable relative positioning.
The grid lines are part of the manifest configuration.

content.explanation: He clarified that the nine-section grid used for explanation is an imaginary aid for understanding positions and is not something to be drawn in Android Studio.
hints: He said 'don't try to put these lines over Android Studio'.
They are conceptual, not actual UI elements.
